solution:
Add corresponding entries in each order.

\(A + B = \begin{bmatrix} 2 + (-1) & -3 + 2 \\ 5 + 2 & -4 + 2 \\ -6 + 0 & 1 + 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 7 & -2 \\ -6 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(B + A = \begin{bmatrix} -1 + 2 & 2 + (-3) \\ 2 + 5 & 2 + (-4) \\ 0 + (-6) & 3 + 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 7 & -2 \\ -6 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\)

The two results agree entry by entry (addition of real numbers is commutative), hence \(A + B = B + A\).

First bracket the left side. \(A + B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ 7 & -2 \\ -6 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\), so

\((A + B) + C = \begin{bmatrix} 1 + 4 & -1 + 3 \\ 7 + (-1) & -2 + 4 \\ -6 + (-2) & 4 + 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 6 & 2 \\ -8 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\)

Now bracket the right side. \(B + C = \begin{bmatrix} -1 + 4 & 2 + 3 \\ 2 + (-1) & 2 + 4 \\ 0 + (-2) & 3 + 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 5 \\ 1 & 6 \\ -2 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\), so

\(A + (B + C) = \begin{bmatrix} 2 + 3 & -3 + 5 \\ 5 + 1 & -4 + 6 \\ -6 + (-2) & 1 + 4 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 6 & 2 \\ -8 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\)

Both groupings give \(\begin{bmatrix} 5 & 2 \\ 6 & 2 \\ -8 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\), hence \((A + B) + C = A + (B + C)\).

\(A + B + C = O\) gives \(C = -(A + B)\).

\(A + B = \begin{bmatrix} 1 + 9 & 2 - 1 & -3 + 2 \\ -3 - 4 & 7 + 2 & -8 + 5 \\ 0 + 4 & -6 + 0 & 1 - 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 10 & 1 & -1 \\ -7 & 9 & -3 \\ 4 & -6 & -2 \end{bmatrix}\)

Changing the sign of every entry,

\(C = \begin{bmatrix} -10 & -1 & 1 \\ 7 & -9 & 3 \\ -4 & 6 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\)

From \(3A - 4B + 5X = C\) we get \(5X = C - 3A + 4B\).

\(3A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -6 \\ 9 & -15 \\ -18 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), \(4B = \begin{bmatrix} -4 & -8 \\ 16 & 8 \\ 4 & 20 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(5X = \begin{bmatrix} 2 - 3 - 4 & 4 + 6 - 8 \\ -1 - 9 + 16 & -4 + 15 + 8 \\ -3 + 18 + 4 & 6 - 0 + 20 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -5 & 2 \\ 6 & 19 \\ 19 & 26 \end{bmatrix}\)

Multiplying by \(\frac{1}{5}\),

\(X = \begin{bmatrix} -1 & \frac{2}{5} \\ \frac{6}{5} & \frac{19}{5} \\ \frac{19}{5} & \frac{26}{5} \end{bmatrix}\)
_note: The printed stem carries a doubled equals sign, "C = = [matrix]", before the third matrix; the intended reading is simply \(C = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 4 \\ -1 & -4 \\ -3 & 6 \end{bmatrix}\). Solving that form reproduces the book's printed answer exactly, so the extra sign is a typesetting slip only, not a lost term.

solution:
Multiply the first equation by 3 and subtract the second to eliminate \(Y\).

\(9X - 3Y = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -3 \\ -3 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\), and subtracting \(X - 3Y = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 0 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\) gives \(8X = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -2 \\ -3 & 4 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(X = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{3}{8} & -\frac{1}{4} \\ -\frac{3}{8} & \frac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix}\)

Now \(Y = 3X - \begin{bmatrix} 1 & -1 \\ -1 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{9}{8} - 1 & -\frac{3}{4} + 1 \\ -\frac{9}{8} + 1 & \frac{3}{2} - 1 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(X = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{3}{8} & -\frac{1}{4} \\ -\frac{3}{8} & \frac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix}\), \(Y = \begin{bmatrix} \frac{1}{8} & \frac{1}{4} \\ -\frac{1}{8} & \frac{1}{2} \end{bmatrix}\)

Multiply the first equation by 2 and subtract the second to eliminate \(B\).

\(4A - 2B = \begin{bmatrix} 12 & -12 & 0 \\ -8 & 4 & 2 \end{bmatrix}\), and subtracting \(A - 2B = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 2 & 8 \\ -2 & 1 & -7 \end{bmatrix}\) gives \(3A = \begin{bmatrix} 9 & -14 & -8 \\ -6 & 3 & 9 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -\frac{14}{3} & -\frac{8}{3} \\ -2 & 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\)

Then \(B = 2A - \begin{bmatrix} 6 & -6 & 0 \\ -4 & 2 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 6 - 6 & -\frac{28}{3} + 6 & -\frac{16}{3} - 0 \\ -4 + 4 & 2 - 2 & 6 - 1 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(A = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & -\frac{14}{3} & -\frac{8}{3} \\ -2 & 1 & 3 \end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & -\frac{10}{3} & -\frac{16}{3} \\ 0 & 0 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\)

Multiply each matrix by its scalar.

\(\cos\theta \begin{bmatrix} \cos\theta & \sin\theta \\ -\sin\theta & \cos\theta \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \cos^2\theta & \sin\theta\cos\theta \\ -\sin\theta\cos\theta & \cos^2\theta \end{bmatrix}\)

\(\sin\theta \begin{bmatrix} \sin\theta & -\cos\theta \\ \cos\theta & \sin\theta \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} \sin^2\theta & -\sin\theta\cos\theta \\ \sin\theta\cos\theta & \sin^2\theta \end{bmatrix}\)

Adding, the off-diagonal terms cancel and each diagonal entry becomes \(\cos^2\theta + \sin^2\theta = 1\).

\(\begin{bmatrix} 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 \end{bmatrix} = I\)

\(A + B = \begin{bmatrix} i + 2i & 2i + i \\ -3 + 2 & 2 - 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3i & 3i \\ -1 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\)

\(A - B = \begin{bmatrix} i - 2i & 2i - i \\ -3 - 2 & 2 + 3 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} -i & i \\ -5 & 5 \end{bmatrix}\)

A square matrix is singular when its determinant is zero.

\(|A + B| = \begin{vmatrix} 3i & 3i \\ -1 & -1 \end{vmatrix} = (3i)(-1) - (3i)(-1) = -3i + 3i = 0\), so \(A + B\) is singular.

\(|A - B| = \begin{vmatrix} -i & i \\ -5 & 5 \end{vmatrix} = (-i)(5) - (i)(-5) = -5i + 5i = 0\)

Yes, \(A - B\) is also singular, because its determinant is 0 (its two columns are proportional, the second being \(-1\) times the first).

Add the two matrices on the left and equate corresponding entries.

\(\begin{bmatrix} 2x + y - 1 & 5 & 5 \\ 6 & 4y & 7 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 & 5 & 5 \\ 6 & 18 & 7 \end{bmatrix}\)

Four entries match automatically; the remaining two give \(2x + y - 1 = 3\) and \(4y = 18\).

From the second, \(y = \frac{18}{4} = \frac{9}{2}\). Substituting in \(2x + y = 4\): \(2x = 4 - \frac{9}{2} = -\frac{1}{2}\).

\(x = -\frac{1}{4}\), \(y = \frac{9}{2}\)
_note: Flagged at transcription because the answers are non-integral, which is out of character for this exercise. Checked against the book's printed key on the answer page: it prints exactly \(x = -\frac{1}{4}\), \(y = \frac{9}{2}\). So the key SUPPORTS the printed stem — no misprint; the fractional answers are intended.

solution:
Equating corresponding entries of the two equal matrices gives four equations:

\(2a + b = 2\), \(3a - b = 3\), \(c + 2d = 4\), \(2c - d = -1\).

Adding the first two, \(5a = 5\), so \(a = 1\) and \(b = 2 - 2(1) = 0\).

From \(2c - d = -1\), \(d = 2c + 1\); substituting in \(c + 2d = 4\) gives \(c + 4c + 2 = 4\), so \(5c = 2\).

\(a = 1\), \(b = 0\), \(c = \frac{2}{5}\), \(d = \frac{9}{5}\)
_note: As printed the stem opens "If  = [matrix] = [matrix]", leaving a dangling equals sign before the first matrix. The question never refers to that matrix by a name anywhere (it asks only for \(a, b, c, d\)), so the intended statement needs no name at all and is read as the plain matrix equation \(\begin{bmatrix} 2a+b & 3a-b \\ c+2d & 2c-d \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 2 & 3 \\ 4 & -1 \end{bmatrix}\). Solving that form reproduces the book's printed key (\(a=1, b=0, c=\frac{2}{5}, d=\frac{9}{5}\)) exactly, confirming the assumption.

solution:
The increase from July to August is \(B - A\).

\(B - A = \begin{bmatrix} 6650 - 5600 & 7055 - 6750 & 8905 - 8500 \\ 7000 - 6650 & 7500 - 7055 & 10200 - 8905 \end{bmatrix} = \begin{bmatrix} 1050 & 305 & 405 \\ 350 & 445 & 1295 \end{bmatrix}\)

So Suresh's sales rose by Rs. 1050 in Physics, Rs. 305 in Chemistry and Rs. 405 in Mathematics, and Ganesh's by Rs. 350, Rs. 445 and Rs. 1295 respectively.

Total increase: Suresh Rs. 1760 and Ganesh Rs. 2090.

A 10 % profit on the August sales is \(\frac{10}{100} B = 0.1 B\).

\(0.1B = \begin{bmatrix} 665 & 705.50 & 890.50 \\ 700 & 750 & 1020 \end{bmatrix}\)

Suresh's profit is Rs. 665 on Physics, Rs. 705.50 on Chemistry and Rs. 890.50 on Mathematics; Ganesh's profit is Rs. 700, Rs. 750 and Rs. 1020 respectively.
